faqs.question: Do digital nomads have to file US taxes?
faqs.answer: Yes. US citizens and green card holders must file a federal tax return on worldwide income regardless of where they live or work. The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion and Foreign Tax Credit can reduce or eliminate your US tax liability, but the filing obligation remains.

faqs.question: Can I claim the FEIE if I move between countries?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Physical Presence Test only requires 330 full days in foreign countries during any 12-month period—the days do not need to be in the same country. You can qualify while moving between multiple countries. The Bona Fide Residence Test requires establishing residence in one specific foreign country for an uninterrupted period that includes a full calendar year.

faqs.question: Do I owe self-employment tax as a digital nomad?
faqs.answer: Yes, unless a Totalization Agreement applies. The FEIE excludes your income from income tax but does not reduce self-employment tax (Social Security and Medicare). If you are self-employed abroad, you generally still owe SE tax at 15.3% on your net self-employment income. A Totalization Agreement between the US and your country of residence may exempt you if you are paying into that country's social security system.

faqs.question: Which state taxes apply to digital nomads?
faqs.answer: State tax obligations depend on your domicile and residency rules, not where you temporarily work. Some states (California, Virginia, South Carolina) aggressively tax former residents until domicile is formally terminated. Others (Texas, Florida, Nevada) have no income tax. FileAbroad reviews your state ties and recommends a domicile strategy when appropriate.

faqs.question: What if I haven't filed taxes since becoming a nomad?
faqs.answer: The Streamlined Filing Compliance Procedures may be an option if your failure to file was non-willful and you meet the foreign residency requirements. Streamlined Foreign Offshore allows qualifying expats to file 3 years of tax returns and 6 years of FBARs with specified penalty treatment. FileAbroad screens these cases after a paid consultation.

faqs.question: Is my Social Security taxable if I live abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. Up to 85% of your Social Security benefits may be subject to US federal income tax depending on your combined income. Living abroad does not exempt Social Security from taxation. Some foreign countries tax Social Security under their local laws, but the US has treaties or totalization agreements with many countries that prevent double taxation.

faqs.question: How are foreign pensions taxed in the US?
faqs.answer: Foreign pension income is generally taxable in the US. The tax treatment depends on whether the US has a tax treaty with the pension country, whether the pension is treated as a trust (requiring Forms 3520/3520-A), and whether the pension fund contains PFICs (requiring Form 8621). Some treaties allow deferred taxation until distribution; others require current reporting of employer contributions. This is one of the most complex areas of expat tax.

faqs.question: Can I contribute to an IRA while living abroad?
faqs.answer: You can contribute to a Traditional or Roth IRA from abroad if you have taxable compensation. However, if you exclude all your income under the FEIE, you may not have enough taxable compensation to support an IRA contribution. Many retirees use the Foreign Tax Credit instead of the FEIE to preserve IRA contribution eligibility. The contribution limits for 2025 are $7,000 ($8,000 if age 50+).

faqs.question: Do I still need to take RMDs from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. Required Minimum Distributions from traditional IRAs, 401(k)s, and similar retirement plans still apply regardless of where you live. The penalty for missing an RMD is 25% of the amount that should have been withdrawn (reduced to 10% if corrected within two years under SECURE 2.0). FileAbroad calculates RMDs and includes them in your annual filing scope.

faqs.question: Will I lose Medicare if I move abroad?
faqs.answer: You do not lose Medicare eligibility by moving abroad, but Medicare generally does not cover healthcare outside the US (with limited exceptions near the border or on cruises). Most retirees abroad purchase local health insurance or private expat health coverage. You should carefully evaluate whether to keep paying Medicare Part B premiums ($185/month in 2025) while abroad, as discontinuing them may result in lifelong late-enrollment penalties.

faqs.question: What is an accidental American?
faqs.answer: An accidental American is someone who acquired US citizenship at birth (usually by being born in the United States to non-US parents, or by having a US citizen parent) but has never lived in the US or considered themselves American. The US taxes its citizens on worldwide income regardless of residence, which means accidental Americans often discover filing obligations only when a foreign bank asks for a US tax identification number.

faqs.question: Do accidental Americans really have to file US taxes?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under current US law, citizenship-based taxation applies to all US citizens, including those who have never lived in the US. There is no exception for accidental Americans. However, the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion, Foreign Tax Credit, and treaty benefits often reduce or eliminate any actual US tax liability. The filing obligation remains even when no tax is owed.

faqs.question: What if I have never filed and don't have a Social Security Number?
faqs.answer: You will need to apply for a Social Security Number (SSN) or an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) before you can file. ITIN applications can be submitted from abroad with your tax return (Form W-7). The process requires certified copies of your passport and can take several weeks to months. FileAbroad can coordinate ITIN application preparation within an accepted scope.

faqs.question: Can I use the Streamlined Procedures as an accidental American?
faqs.answer: Many accidental Americans qualify for the Streamlined Foreign Offshore Procedures if their failure to file was non-willful and they meet the foreign residency requirements. Streamlined allows qualifying taxpayers to file 3 years of tax returns and 6 years of FBARs with specified penalty treatment. You must certify non-willfulness under penalties of perjury. FileAbroad screens these cases after a paid consultation.

faqs.question: Should I renounce my US citizenship?
faqs.answer: Renunciation is a permanent, irrevocable decision with significant legal, travel, and financial consequences. Before renouncing, you must be compliant with US tax filing for the 5 years prior to renunciation. If your net worth exceeds $2 million or your average annual net income tax liability exceeds certain thresholds, you may be a 'covered expatriate' subject to exit tax (Form 8854). FileAbroad can review your facts and refer you to qualified legal counsel for the renunciation decision itself.

faqs.question: Do I need to file Form 5471 for my foreign corporation?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you are a US person who owns 10% or more of a foreign corporation, or if the corporation is a Controlled Foreign Corporation (CFC) and you are a US shareholder. Form 5471 reports the corporation's income, balance sheet, and your share of Subpart F and GILTI income.

faqs.question: What is GILTI and does it apply to me?
faqs.answer: Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI) is a US tax on certain income earned by Controlled Foreign Corporations (CFCs) that exceeds a 10% return on tangible assets. If you own a CFC, you may have a GILTI inclusion on your personal tax return. A Section 962 election can reduce the tax rate.

faqs.question: Should I form a foreign LLC or a foreign corporation?
faqs.answer: The optimal structure depends on your income level, foreign tax rate, and long-term goals. A foreign LLC may be classified as a disregarded entity, partnership, or corporation for US tax purposes. A foreign corporation may trigger CFC and GILTI rules. Each structure has different reporting and tax implications.

faqs.question: Can I avoid US tax on my foreign business income?
faqs.answer: Generally no. US citizens and residents are taxed on worldwide income, including income from foreign businesses. The FEIE may exclude earned income up to the limit, but it does not apply to business profits distributed as dividends. The Foreign Tax Credit can reduce double taxation. Proper entity structuring is essential.

faqs.question: Do I need to file Form 8865 for my foreign partnership?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you are a US person with an interest in a foreign partnership. Form 8865 reports the partnership's income, deductions, and your share of partnership items. If the partnership has US effectively connected income, Section 1446 withholding may also apply.

faqs.question: How are crypto gains taxed for US expats?
faqs.answer: Crypto gains are taxed as capital gains (short-term or long-term) for US taxpayers regardless of where you live. Short-term gains (held less than one year) are taxed at ordinary income rates. Long-term gains (held more than one year) are taxed at preferential rates (0%, 15%, or 20%). Foreign tax credits may apply if you paid tax to your country of residence.

faqs.question: Do I need to report crypto on FBAR?
faqs.answer: It depends. If your crypto is held on a foreign exchange that is considered a foreign financial institution, and the aggregate value of all your foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000, you must file FBAR. Crypto held in personal wallets (non-custodial) is generally not reportable on FBAR but may be reportable on Form 8938 if thresholds are met.

faqs.question: How are staking rewards and DeFi yields taxed?
faqs.answer: Staking rewards and DeFi yields are generally taxed as ordinary income at fair market value when received. Subsequent sales of the rewarded tokens trigger capital gains or losses. The IRS has issued guidance that treats staking rewards as income, but the exact characterization of DeFi yields (interest, rental, or other) depends on the specific protocol.

faqs.question: Do I pay tax in my country of residence on crypto gains?
faqs.answer: It depends on your country of residence. Some countries tax crypto gains as capital gains, others as ordinary income, and some have no crypto tax at all. You may be able to claim a foreign tax credit on your US return for crypto tax paid abroad. Proper documentation of foreign tax paid is essential.

faqs.question: What records do I need for crypto tax reporting?
faqs.answer: You need a complete transaction history including: date of each acquisition and disposition, fair market value in USD at the time of transaction, cost basis, fees, and the character of each transaction (trade, staking, mining, airdrop, etc.). Most exchanges provide CSV exports. Third-party tools like CoinTracker or Koinly can help organize the data.

faqs.question: Do green card holders have to file US taxes from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. US permanent residents (green card holders) are subject to US tax on worldwide income regardless of where they live. This is the same rule that applies to US citizens. The FEIE, FTC, and treaty benefits are available to green card holders just as they are to citizens.

faqs.question: Does an expired green card affect my tax obligations?
faqs.answer: An expired green card does not automatically end your US tax obligations. You remain a lawful permanent resident for tax purposes until your status is formally terminated by USCIS or a court. If your green card has expired and you have been absent from the US for an extended period, consult an immigration attorney about your status.

faqs.question: What is the exit tax for green card holders?
faqs.answer: Green card holders who are 'long-term residents' (held green card status in 8 of the last 15 years) may be subject to the exit tax when they abandon their green card. The exit tax applies if you are a 'covered expatriate' based on net worth, average tax liability, or tax compliance certification. Form 8854 is required.

faqs.question: Can green card holders claim the FEIE?
faqs.answer: Yes. Green card holders can claim the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion if they meet the Physical Presence Test or Bona Fide Residence Test, just like US citizens. The FEIE limit for 2025 is $130,000 per person.

faqs.question: Should I abandon my green card or naturalize?
faqs.answer: This is a personal and legal decision with significant tax implications. Naturalization makes you a US citizen permanently subject to US tax and exit tax. Abandoning a green card may trigger exit tax if you are a long-term resident. Consult both an immigration attorney and a tax specialist before deciding.

faqs.question: Is combat zone pay taxable?
faqs.answer: No. Military pay received while serving in a combat zone is excluded from gross income for federal tax purposes. This includes basic pay, reenlistment bonuses, and incentive pay. Officers are limited to the highest enlisted pay plus imminent danger pay. The exclusion does not apply to civilian contractors.

faqs.question: Can contractors claim the FEIE?
faqs.answer: It depends. Contractors working overseas may qualify for the FEIE if they meet the Physical Presence Test or Bona Fide Residence Test. However, if you are working on a US military base and your tax home is considered to be in the US, you may not qualify. Each case requires individual analysis.

faqs.question: How does the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act affect state taxes?
faqs.answer: The SCRA allows military personnel to maintain their state of legal residence (domicile) for tax purposes regardless of where they are stationed. If your legal residence is a no-income-tax state like Texas or Florida, you can avoid state income tax even if stationed in a high-tax state. This does not apply to civilian contractors.

faqs.question: Do I owe state tax if I am stationed abroad?
faqs.answer: For military personnel, state tax depends on your state of legal residence (domicile), not your duty station. If your domicile is a state with income tax, you may owe state tax. If your domicile is a no-tax state, you generally do not. Civilian contractors are subject to the state tax rules of their actual state of residence.

faqs.question: Can I exclude housing allowances from tax?
faqs.answer: Military Basic Allowance for Housing (BAH) and Overseas Housing Allowance (OHA) are generally not taxable for military personnel. Civilian contractors do not receive these military-specific exclusions, but they may qualify for the Foreign Housing Exclusion or Deduction under the FEIE if eligible.

faqs.question: Do freelancers have to pay self-employment tax abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. Self-employed Americans abroad must pay US self-employment tax (15.3%) on net earnings unless a Totalization Agreement exempts them. The FEIE excludes income from income tax but does not reduce self-employment tax. Most countries popular with freelancers do not have Totalization Agreements with the US.

faqs.question: Can I claim the FEIE on freelance income?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you meet the Physical Presence Test or Bona Fide Residence Test. Freelance income is considered earned income and qualifies for the FEIE. However, the FEIE does not apply to passive income (dividends, interest, capital gains) or to income earned in the US.

faqs.question: Do I need to make quarterly estimated tax payments from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you expect to owe at least $1,000 in tax for the year after subtracting withholding and credits. Quarterly payments are due April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15. You can pay electronically from abroad using EFTPS or Direct Pay.

faqs.question: Can I deduct home office expenses from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you use part of your foreign home exclusively and regularly for business. You can deduct a portion of rent, utilities, and other housing expenses. The foreign housing deduction (Form 2555) is available if you are self-employed and claim the FEIE.

faqs.question: Do I need a foreign business entity?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Many freelancers operate as sole proprietors (Schedule C). However, forming a foreign entity may provide liability protection, local tax benefits, or Totalization Agreement advantages. The US tax implications of foreign entities are complex and require professional analysis.

faqs.question: Does teaching income qualify for the FEIE?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you meet the Physical Presence Test or Bona Fide Residence Test. Teaching income is earned income and qualifies for the FEIE. Many teachers on multi-year contracts can establish bona fide residence, while those on shorter contracts may use the Physical Presence Test.

faqs.question: How is employer-provided housing taxed?
faqs.answer: If your school provides housing, the fair market value of the housing is generally taxable income. However, the Foreign Housing Exclusion (Form 2555) may exclude a portion of the housing cost if you qualify for the FEIE. The exclusion is limited to 30% of the FEIE limit ($39,870 for 2025) minus a base amount ($20,240).

faqs.question: Are teacher pensions from abroad taxable in the US?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, unless a tax treaty exempts them. Many US tax treaties have provisions for government service pensions or teacher pensions. For example, the US-UK treaty generally exempts UK teacher pensions from US tax if the recipient is a UK resident. Each treaty is different and requires individual analysis.

faqs.question: Can I contribute to a 403(b) or IRA while teaching abroad?
faqs.answer: You can contribute to an IRA if you have taxable compensation. However, if you exclude all your income under the FEIE, you may not have enough taxable compensation to support a contribution. Many teachers use the Foreign Tax Credit instead of the FEIE to preserve IRA contribution eligibility.

faqs.question: Do teachers get any special tax treaty benefits?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many US tax treaties have specific articles for teachers and researchers that exempt teaching income from host-country tax for a limited period (typically 2 years). This does not exempt the income from US tax, but it may reduce or eliminate foreign tax, making the FEIE or FTC more valuable.

faqs.question: Do dual citizens have to file US taxes?
faqs.answer: Yes. US citizens, including dual citizens, are subject to US tax on worldwide income regardless of where they live. Your foreign citizenship does not eliminate your US tax obligations. However, tax treaties, the FEIE, and the FTC can reduce or eliminate double taxation.

faqs.question: Which country taxes my income first?
faqs.answer: It depends on the type of income and the tax treaty. Generally, employment income is taxed in the country of residence, business profits are taxed where the business is located, and passive income (dividends, interest) is taxed in the source country with a foreign tax credit available in the residence country. Each treaty article addresses specific income types.

faqs.question: Can I renounce my US citizenship to avoid US tax?
faqs.answer: Renunciation eliminates future US tax obligations but may trigger the exit tax if you are a covered expatriate. It is a permanent, irrevocable decision with significant legal and travel consequences. You must also be compliant with US tax filing for the 5 years prior to renunciation. Consult an immigration attorney and tax specialist before deciding.

faqs.question: Do I need to report foreign accounts on FBAR?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the aggregate value of all your foreign financial accounts exceeded $10,000 at any time during the year. This applies to all US persons, including dual citizens. FBAR is filed separately from your tax return and has its own penalties.

faqs.question: Can I use a foreign tax credit for tax paid to my other country?
faqs.answer: Yes. The US Foreign Tax Credit allows you to claim a dollar-for-dollar credit for income taxes paid to a foreign country. This prevents double taxation on the same income. The credit is limited to the US tax liability on foreign-source income. Excess credits can be carried forward 10 years.

faqs.question: Can I file jointly with my foreign spouse?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you make the non-resident alien spouse election under Section 6013(g). This election treats your foreign spouse as a US resident for tax purposes, allowing you to file jointly. The election applies to the current year and all future years until revoked. Both spouses must report worldwide income.

faqs.question: Does my foreign spouse need an ITIN?
faqs.answer: If you file jointly, your foreign spouse needs an ITIN (Individual Taxpayer Identification Number). You can apply for an ITIN by filing Form W-7 with your tax return. The process requires certified copies of your spouse's passport and can take several weeks.

faqs.question: Do I report my foreign spouse's accounts on FBAR?
faqs.answer: It depends. If you have signature authority or a financial interest in your spouse's foreign accounts, you must report them on FBAR. Joint accounts are always reportable. Accounts solely in your spouse's name are generally not reportable by you, but may be reportable by your spouse if they are a US person.

faqs.question: Can I gift assets to my foreign spouse?
faqs.answer: Yes, but special rules apply. For 2025, you can gift up to $185,000 per year to a non-citizen spouse without gift tax (this is a separate limit from the unlimited marital deduction for citizen spouses). Gifts above this amount require filing Form 709 and may consume your lifetime exemption ($13.99 million for 2025).

faqs.question: How does my foreign spouse's income affect my US tax?
faqs.answer: If you file separately, your foreign spouse's income generally does not affect your US tax. If you file jointly (via the 6013(g) election), you must include your spouse's worldwide income on your joint return. This may increase your tax liability but also provides access to higher standard deductions and lower joint tax brackets.

faqs.question: Is YouTube income self-employment income?
faqs.answer: Generally yes. Income from YouTube AdSense, sponsorships, and brand deals is typically treated as self-employment income (Schedule C) if you are actively creating content. Passive income from pre-existing content with minimal ongoing effort may be treated as royalty income. The distinction affects self-employment tax and deduction eligibility.

faqs.question: Can I deduct content creation expenses?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ordinary and necessary business expenses are deductible, including camera equipment, software subscriptions, internet costs, travel for content creation, and home office expenses. Keep detailed records and receipts. Equipment over $2,500 per item may need to be depreciated rather than expensed immediately.

faqs.question: Do I pay tax in my country of residence on content income?
faqs.answer: It depends on your country of residence. Most countries tax residents on worldwide income, including content creation income from US platforms. You may be able to claim a foreign tax credit on your US return for tax paid to your country of residence. Proper documentation is essential.

faqs.question: Should I form an LLC or corporation for my content business?
faqs.answer: An LLC can provide liability protection and may offer tax benefits, but it also adds complexity (separate tax return, payroll if you have employees). For most solo creators, operating as a sole proprietor (Schedule C) is simplest. Consider an LLC once your income exceeds $75,000-$100,000 annually or you have significant liability risk.

faqs.question: How do I report cryptocurrency payments from sponsors?
faqs.answer: Crypto payments are taxable as ordinary income at fair market value when received. You must report the USD equivalent on your tax return. Subsequent changes in the crypto's value trigger capital gains or losses when you sell or exchange it. Keep detailed records of the date, amount, and fair market value of each crypto payment.
